The full-length interview with Elon Musk | The Economist youtu.be/XuoqKYxDHVc?si=ut_J… via @YouTube   Overall summary  Elon Musk’s @elonmusk central argument is that artificial intelligence and humanoid robotics are approaching a technological singularity that will overwhelm almost every other economic and political issue within the next decade. He predicts that AI could exceed the combined intelligence of humanity within roughly five years and become vastly more intelligent than humans by 2036. Once that digital intelligence is connected to large numbers of capable humanoid robots, Musk believes society could enter an “age of amazing abundance” in which machines produce goods and services at such enormous scale that conventional scarcity, employment and even money gradually become less important.  00:00–12:00: AI, robots and the end of scarcity  Musk begins by describing himself as an instinctive builder and tries to connect Tesla, SpaceX, xAI and humanoid robotics within one overarching vision. AI currently operates mainly in the digital realm, but robots would give that intelligence the ability to manipulate the physical world. In his framework, an economy is simply the production of goods and the provision of services; therefore, if billions of intelligent robots can perform both functions, economic output could become almost unlimited.  This is the basis for Musk’s striking prediction that “money won’t matter in 2036.” He argues that people ultimately want money because it allows them to obtain housing, food, transport, entertainment and other services. If machines can produce more of these things than humans could possibly consume, money would lose much of its traditional purpose. The interviewer, Zanny Minton Beddoes, repeatedly brings him back to practical questions such as who will own the robots and how his companies will make money, but Musk’s answer remains largely post-scarcity and philosophical rather than a conventional business forecast.  12:00–27:30: AI risk, China and governance  Musk acknowledges that humans may eventually lose control over systems that become vastly more intelligent than themselves. He compares the potential relationship between superintelligent AI and humanity with the relationship between humans and chimpanzees, noting that chimpanzees clearly do not control human civilization.  What is striking is how much his attitude toward AI risk appears to have changed. Musk previously warned about recursive self-improvement and estimated a meaningful probability of catastrophic outcomes, including “killer robots.” In this interview, he does not withdraw those concerns, but concludes that AI development has acquired so much momentum that it probably cannot be stopped. His philosophy is essentially that humanity should attempt to shape the process toward a positive outcome while accepting that the process itself is inevitable. As he puts it, the most likely outcome is abundance, so he would probably not press a hypothetical button that permanently stopped AI development.  On safety, Musk proposes regular coordination among the leading AI laboratories. Competing developers could test one another’s frontier models, identify vulnerabilities and recommend delays when they discover serious risks. Despite his personal conflicts with figures such as Sam Altman, Musk says that these differences could be set aside when the safety of advanced AI is involved. Governments, particularly the United States and China, should intervene if companies knowingly release systems that present unacceptable dangers.  Musk is also unusually direct about China’s competitive position. He argues that AI leadership will ultimately be constrained by chips, electricity, cooling and robotics. China already has enormous power-generation capacity, a strong manufacturing ecosystem and increasingly capable robot companies. Export restrictions may constrain China’s access to advanced chips, but they cannot stop the rest of the world from using competitive Chinese models. In Musk’s view, restricting American companies from accessing Chinese models would not prevent China from eventually becoming an AI leader.  This is one of the interview’s most important investment insights: Musk does not view the AI race purely as a model-quality or semiconductor contest. He views it as a physical infrastructure race involving electricity, data centers, cooling systems, chips, factories and eventually enormous robot fleets.  27:30–40:40: Jobs, universal income and deflation  Musk expects the transition to be economically disruptive. He says AI will soon outperform humans in virtually every job performed through a computer or phone, and claims that AI is already better at programming than the large majority of software engineers. He expects performance to eventually reach what he calls “Stockfish level,” referring to chess software that is so superior that even the best human players cannot compete.  Physical jobs will take longer because they require capable robots, but Musk believes humanoid robotics will eventually remove that limitation. His conclusion is that work will become optional. He compares future employment with gardening: people may still work because they enjoy the activity or value something made by a human, but they will no longer need to work to obtain basic goods and services.  Minton Beddoes presses him on the transition, which is arguably the weakest part of Musk’s thesis. Even if technological abundance eventually arrives, millions of workers could lose their incomes long before abundance is distributed evenly. Musk suggests that the US Treasury could simply issue people checks. When challenged that this would be inflationary, he argues that inflation depends on the relationship between money and real output. If AI and robots increase the supply of goods and services faster than the government increases the money supply, the result would be deflation rather than inflation.  The logic is economically coherent at the endpoint, but the interview leaves the transition problem largely unresolved. Musk describes an extraordinary destination, but offers less detail on how societies move from today’s labor-dependent economy to that destination without severe unemployment, political backlash, wealth concentration or instability. Minton Beddoes repeatedly identifies this gap, describing the future as both exhilarating and frightening.  40:40–49:36: Concentrated power and founder control  The conversation then turns to Musk’s extraordinary control over his companies. He argues that concentrated voting power is necessary because public markets pressure management teams to optimize quarterly earnings rather than invest in projects whose returns may take five, ten or twenty years to emerge.  SpaceX may spend huge sums on the Moon, Mars and Starship infrastructure while depressing near-term profitability. Musk does not want shareholders or short sellers to prevent those investments merely because quarterly margins disappoint. He therefore presents founder control not primarily as a mechanism for personal enrichment, but as protection for long-duration technological missions. He also praises retail investors, whom he believes are often more patient and strategically minded than institutional investors.  However, the interviewer raises the obvious governance concern: a small number of unelected founders now control technologies that could shape communication networks, warfare, artificial intelligence and eventually the global economy. Musk’s response is largely that concentrated power has always existed and that his companies need consistent long-term direction.  49:36–55:00: Starlink, Ukraine and private geopolitical power  Starlink illustrates the governance dilemma in concrete form. Musk explains that Russian forces had obtained Starlink terminals through indirect channels and were using them in occupied Ukrainian territory. SpaceX worked with the Ukrainian government to create a whitelist of authorized terminals, although this also disconnected some innocent civilian users.  Minton Beddoes asks whether it is appropriate for one businessman to possess infrastructure capable of influencing the direction of a war. Musk disputes the idea that he personally determines military outcomes, but acknowledges Starlink’s importance. On Ukraine, he advocates a pragmatic negotiated settlement, arguing that front lines have moved relatively little while both sides continue suffering heavy casualties. He believes Ukraine is unlikely to retake all occupied territories and that insisting on complete Russian withdrawal could prolong the war without changing the eventual result.  55:00–61:00: DOGE, the US deficit and USAID  Musk admits that he “got a little too involved in politics” and “got carried away.” He nevertheless defends the motivation behind DOGE, arguing that the US fiscal position is unsustainable and that interest payments have become larger than combined spending on major national-security functions. His account portrays DOGE as a basic effort to verify recipients, remove fraud and stop payments that could not be traced to their intended beneficiaries.  The most contentious exchange concerns cuts to USAID and foreign-assistance programs. Minton Beddoes argues that abruptly terminating health funding almost certainly caused unnecessary suffering and potentially deaths, particularly when programs supplying essential medicines were suddenly disrupted. Musk categorically rejects this and says that “zero” people died because of DOGE, arguing that private foundations and other nongovernmental organizations could have filled legitimate funding gaps.  The two do not reach agreement. Musk views much of the system as wasteful, fraudulent or politically motivated; Minton Beddoes accepts that waste existed but argues that dismantling programs without an orderly transition imposed real human costs.  61:00–83:00: Europe, immigration and political polarization  The final major section becomes openly adversarial. Minton Beddoes challenges Musk over his support for European populist and far-right political movements, his claims about crime and immigration, and his prediction that civil war in Britain is eventually inevitable.  Musk rejects the “far-right” label and describes his positions as centrist: secure borders, safe cities and responsible government spending. He argues that views considered mainstream ten or fifteen years ago are now misleadingly portrayed as extremist. He believes Europe’s welfare systems create powerful incentives for uncontrolled migration and warns that admitting large populations with values that conflict with liberal Western norms could eventually produce severe social instability.  Minton Beddoes agrees that borders should be controlled and that integration matters, but accuses Musk of exaggerating Europe’s problems, amplifying extreme actors and presenting a distorted picture to hundreds of millions of followers. She argues that immigration also brings significant economic advantages to an aging continent and that the United Kingdom has generally integrated immigrants more successfully than Musk acknowledges.  The disagreement is therefore not simply over whether Europe has problems. Both accept that migration must be managed. The disagreement concerns magnitude, evidence and rhetoric. Musk believes establishment institutions are ignoring a civilizational threat; Minton Beddoes believes Musk’s inflammatory interventions could intensify the very polarization and violence he claims to fear.  Musk insists that his politics are centrist and that history will vindicate his predictions. He characterizes himself as unusually capable of seeing future developments before the wider public recognizes them, while acknowledging that his timing is not always correct.  83:00–85:21: The final conclusion  The interview ends where it began, with AI. Musk argues that superintelligence is called a singularity precisely because developments beyond that point cannot be reliably predicted. Whatever happens with elections, immigration or geopolitical disputes, he believes AI and robots will dominate the world’s major economic and political outcomes within less than ten years.  That is the unifying idea behind the entire interview: Musk believes almost everyone is thinking too incrementally. Governments are debating deficits, borders, jobs and elections using assumptions formed in the industrial era, while AI and robotics may soon rewrite the basic relationships among intelligence, labor, production, money and political power.  Bottom line  The interview presents Musk at his most visionary and his most controversial. On AI, infrastructure, robotics and long-term technological change, he offers a coherent and genuinely important framework: intelligence is becoming abundant, physical production will follow once robotics scales, and energy and compute will become the strategic resources of the next era.  His analysis becomes less convincing when addressing the transition from technological abundance to broadly shared prosperity. Saying that work, taxation and money may eventually become irrelevant does not explain what happens during the years when labor income disappears faster than ownership and purchasing power are redistributed.  The sharpest contrast in the interview is therefore between Musk the engineer and Musk the political actor. The engineer identifies bottlenecks, extrapolates technological curves and thinks in decades. The political actor relies far more heavily on personal conviction, social-media evidence and sweeping claims that the interviewer repeatedly challenges. Both versions of Musk are visible throughout the discussion, which is exactly what makes the interview so fascinating.

AI Is Not the End of Work. It May Be the Beginning of a More Human Future.  In 2020, the world experienced something it had not planned for: a global pause.  COVID-19 disrupted almost every system we had built. Offices emptied. Commutes disappeared. Meetings moved online. Families adapted. Industries changed overnight.  But something else happened.  For the first time in generations, millions of people were forced to question the machine we had created around ourselves.  Why were we working longer hours than ever? Why did being constantly busy become a symbol of success? Why did exhaustion become something to be proud of? The pandemic revealed something many people already felt but rarely said out loud: We are tired.  The modern world was built on the idea that human productivity could always increase. More emails. More meetings. More tasks. More output. More pressure.  But humans are not machines. We have limits.  This is where artificial intelligence enters the conversation.  Many people see AI as a threat because they imagine a future where machines replace people. But another possibility exists: AI could become one of humanity’s greatest tools for reducing the burden we placed on ourselves.  AI can handle repetitive tasks. AI can help people organise information. AI can assist creators, researchers, teachers, doctors, and workers.  The goal should not be replacing humans.  The goal should be giving humans back something we have slowly lost: time. Time to think. Time to create. Time to spend with family. Time to learn. Time to live. Throughout history, technology has changed the way humans work. The printing press changed knowledge. Electricity changed industry. Computers changed information.  AI is another turning point.  The question is not whether AI will change the world. It already is.  The real question is whether we use it to push humans harder, or whether we finally use technology to give people room to breathe. Maybe the future of AI is not a world where humans work less because machines have taken over. Maybe it is a world where humans can finally focus on the things machines were never meant to replace.

Good morning from Virginia. 🇺🇸  On this day in 1964, the Gulf of Tonkin incident began—an event that would dramatically expand America’s role in Vietnam.  On the afternoon of August 2, the destroyer USS Maddox was on an intelligence patrol in international waters when three North Vietnamese torpedo boats attacked. The Maddox opened fire with her 5-inch guns as the boats closed and launched torpedoes. Carrier aircraft from the USS Ticonderoga joined the fight. One boat was left dead in the water; the others fled damaged. The Maddox took only a single machine-gun bullet.  Two nights later, under heavy weather and darkness, the Maddox and USS Turner Joy reported a second attack. Radar contacts and sonar reports of torpedo wakes filled the night. The ships zigzagged and poured hundreds of rounds into the darkness. Yet even as the engagement unfolded, Captain John Herrick sent a flash message that still echoes:  “Review of action makes many reported contacts and torpedoes fired appear doubtful. Freak weather effects on radar and overeager sonarmen may have accounted for many reports. No actual visual sightings by MADDOX. Suggest complete evaluation before any further action taken.”  Washington did not wait. That same night President Lyndon Johnson told the nation:  “Renewed hostile actions against United States ships on the high seas in the Gulf of Tonkin have today required me to order the military forces of the United States to take action in reply… Repeated acts of violence against the Armed Forces of the United States must be met not only with alert defense, but with positive reply.”  He ordered airstrikes on North Vietnamese patrol boat bases. Within days Congress passed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, giving the President authority “to take all necessary measures to repel any armed attack against the forces of the United States and to prevent further aggression.”  The first clash was real. The second almost certainly never happened—a deadly mix of weather, radar ghosts, and the fog of war. Yet that incomplete information became the legal foundation for a war that would cost more than 58,000 American lives.  History rarely offers clean lessons. This one demands we remember both the courage of the men on those destroyers and the speed with which uncertainty can commit a nation to years of costly struggle.  America 250 🇺🇸

In August 2022, NCBA Bank’s head of security and investigations flagged a major risk on the Fuliza platform. Analysts detected a sharp, highly localized surge in unpaid mobile-money overdrafts. More than 123,000 newly activated Safaricom SIM cards—mostly registered around January 2022—had opted into Fuliza, drawn their full limits, and then gone permanently offline. Attempts at routine debt recovery failed because every line had been deactivated or discarded, leaving NCBA with a loss of approximately 449 million shillings. The bank formally referred the matter to the DCI Banking Fraud Investigation Unit (BFIU). Detectives traced the scheme to the generation of tens of thousands of falsified National Registration Bureau identity numbers. The syndicate injected fictional identities (names, photos, and biometric templates) into the national registration systems at a root level. These “ghost” profiles were treated as legitimate by the database, allowing official ID numbers to be issued for non-existent people. Because the entries bypassed physical vetting, chief’s letters, and fingerprint checks, external systems—including banks and mobile operators—accepted them as genuine when performing KYC checks. Armed with these authentic-looking but fictitious IDs, the group mass-registered over 123,000 Safaricom lines and opened associated bank accounts. They first ran a controlled “borrow-and-repay” cycle on each line to raise Fuliza limits, then executed a coordinated sweep that maxed out the overdrafts across thousands of accounts in a short window, generating unrepayable debt. The proceeds were layered through secondary burner SIMs, fragmented across more than 35,000 M-Pesa agent outlets in small withdrawals to avoid AML triggers, and later deposited into bank accounts disguised as legitimate M-Pesa float. Luxury assets—including two new Subaru Foresters, a Toyota Mark X, a Toyota Probox, and motorbikes—were acquired with the funds. In early February 2023, after months of analysis and cell-tower triangulation, the DCI carried out simultaneous raids. Seven suspects (Isaac Kipkemoi, Gideon Rono, Moses Rono, Collins Kipyegon, Maxwell Njamba, Edwin Kipkorir, and Gideon Kirui) were arrested in a rented apartment in Kiamunyi, Nakuru, that functioned as an operational hub. The technical mastermind, Peter Gitahi Wambui, was arrested in Kitale. Seized items included roughly 123,000 SIM cards, more than 200 ATM cards, registration forms, phones, laptops, and routers. The suspects were charged at Milimani Law Courts on 13 February 2023 with 13 counts under the Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act, including conspiracy to steal, stealing, organised criminal activity, and possession of proceeds of crime. The Asset Recovery Agency later obtained High Court orders forfeiting the luxury vehicles and motorbikes to the state as proceeds of the fraud. As of mid-2025 the criminal case remained ongoing.

AI companies are buying large volumes of used, rare, and out-of-print books, scanning them for training data, and in many cases destroying the physical copies afterward.   This practice has accelerated as labs seek high-quality, pre-2022 human-written text free of AI-generated content that now saturates much of the open web.  The most documented example is Anthropic’s internal effort known as Project Panama. Court filings from copyright litigation revealed that the company acquired millions of physical books from used-book sellers and wholesalers such as Better World Books. Workers used hydraulic cutting machines to slice off the spines, fed the loose pages into industrial high-speed scanners, and then discarded or pulped the remains. An internal planning document described the goal as an effort to destructively scan books at massive scale. A federal judge later ruled that purchasing the books, creating internal digital copies this way, and destroying the originals constituted transformative fair use under U.S. copyright law, relying in part on the first-sale doctrine.  Similar activity is now widespread. Specialized brokers, including ISBNdb, openly market bulk acquisition services to AI labs, offering orders ranging from thousands to as many as one million titles. They emphasize older printed books as “structurally clean” training data.   Booksellers in the United States and Europe have reported sudden surges in bulk orders for mixed, random selections that include rare and out-of-print volumes. Some of these titles may represent among the last readily available physical copies. While a substantial portion of the books involved would otherwise have been remaindered, recycled, or sent to landfills, the inclusion of uncommon editions has drawn criticism from archivists, collectors, and rare-book dealers who note that gentler, non-destructive scanning methods exist yet are slower and more expensive.  The process remains largely quiet because the intermediary services promise anonymity to their AI clients. Public attention has grown mainly through litigation disclosures and reporting by outlets that examined the court records and interviewed booksellers.   The practice highlights a practical tension in large-scale AI development: the demand for vast quantities of reliable human text collides with the finite physical supply of older printed works and the cultural value of preserving rare copies.

The post alleges that the data was stolen from the Instituto Nacional de la Seguridad Social (INSS), the country's national social security institute, after extortion attempts failed.  According to the forum listing, the breach involves 3,184,288 records exported in JSON format. The actor claims to have used "TerciosRAT" malware to access the system. The exposed dataset reportedly includes sensitive personally identifiable information (PII) and financial data for each individual, including:  *   Full names *   DNI (National Identity Document) numbers *   Dates of birth *   IBAN (International Bank Account Number) details *   Home addresses *   Landline and mobile phone numbers *   Email addresses *   Number of children  The INSS is a critical government entity in Spain, responsible for managing social security benefits for millions of citizens. A compromise of this scale would expose a significant portion of the elderly population to identity theft, financial fraud, and targeted phishing attacks. The actor stated that they attempted to extort payment to prevent the leak but proceeded with the sale after receiving no response.  At the time of reporting, the alleged breach has not been independently verified by INSS or Spanish cybersecurity authorities.

This is the conventional wisdom: Microsoft should make security features free or include them in lower-tier plans.  Unfortunately, in this specific example from @HackingLZ, moving risk-based Conditional Access to P1 is unlikely to make a significant dent in global security risk.  Why? I spent the better part of three years trying to persuade organizations that already had E5 licenses to enable P2 features. Sadly, very few did. Even though they were already paying for them. Deployment simply required too much work and change management on their end.  My entire team at Microsoft worked with E5 customers, and one of the things we actively tracked and followed up on was the deployment of risk-based Conditional Access policies.  Microsoft even offered incentives to account teams worldwide when the customers they managed enabled risk-based Conditional Access. Yet there were still very few takers.  So, taking a step back: what can Microsoft do to have the greatest impact on the security of all its customers?  My observation was that the biggest improvements came from security features that required customers to do nothing.  The “Microsoft-managed” class of features is what actually moves the needle on security.  Some key initiatives included:  → Blocking legacy authentication protocols for Exchange Online  → Enforcing MFA for Azure (you wouldn’t believe how many enterprises. Even regulated ones, threw the book at us over this)  → Introducing Microsoft-managed Conditional Access policies  → Blocking device code flow by default  The next major effort is disabling SMS and voice-based MFA while rolling out passkeys.  That change alone will improve security for an enormous number of organizations.  These initiatives require a huge amount of time, effort, and follow-up to help customers manage the impact.  Many of the ones listed above were multi-year projects, with some taking three+ years to move the final group of customers across.  In my opinion, it can sometimes be better for more advanced features to remain paid.   Customers recognize them as premium capabilities, pay for them, and 'ideally' commit the resources needed to deploy them properly.

🤖 [GEMINI 분석] 2026-08-02 19:07 KST
🟠 위협 점수: 8/10 (높음)

### 1. 현재 주요 사이버보안 트렌드
최근 사이버 위협 환경은 **Agentic AI**를 활용한 자율적 공격과 기존 공격 기법의 고도화가 결합된 양상을 보입니다. 특히, 공격자들이 **Adform**과 같은 광고 스크립트를 변조하여 암호화폐 지갑 주소를 탈취하거나, **Coldcard** 하드웨어 지갑의 펌웨어 결함을 악용해 대규모 자산을 탈취하는 등 금융 탈취 수법이 정교해지고 있습니다 ([TheHackerNews](https://thehackernews.com/2026/08/coldcard-hardware-wallet-flaw-linked-to.html)). 또한, **Ruby on Rails** 및 **Adobe Campaign Classic**과 같은 엔터프라이즈 플랫폼의 치명적인 취약점이 지속적으로 발견되어 즉각적인 패치 관리가 요구됩니다 ([BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/rails-patches-critical-active-storage-flaw-with-rce-potential/)).

### 2. 주요 위협 행위자 / 캠페인
- **Toy Ghouls**: **GenieLocker** 랜섬웨어를 사용하여 Windows, Linux, ESXi 시스템을 공격하는 금전적 동기 중심의 위협 그룹 ([Securelist](https://securelist.com/genielocker-ransomware-for-windows-linux-and-esxi/120843/)).
- **Larva-26009**: MS-SQL 서버를 타겟으로 **XMRig** 코인 마이너, **VShell**, **GotoHTTP**를 설치하여 시스템을 장악하는 공격자 ([AhnLab ASEC](https://asec.ahnlab.com/ko/94684/)).
- **ShinyHunters**: 글로벌 기업 및 비영리 기관을 대상으로 데이터 유출을 주장하며 협박하는 활동 포착 ([AhnLab ASEC](https://asec.ahnlab.com/ko/94706/)).
- **OctLurk / SilkLurk**: 중앙아시아 지역을 타겟으로 메모리 상주형 백도어를 통해 자격 증명 탈취 및 네트워크 스캔을 수행하는 사이버 스파이 그룹 ([Securelist](https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/)).

### 3. 한국 관련 위협
- **국가배후 해킹조직**: 대한민국 국가정보원, 경찰청 등 합동 권고문에 따르면 2025년부터 2026년 상반기까지 국가배후 해킹 그룹이 국내 기업을 대상으로 **Gunra** 랜섬웨어 공격을 수행한 정황이 확인됨 ([AhnLab ASEC](https://asec.ahnlab.com/ko/94684/)).
- **피싱 공격**: 국세청 세무 위반 통지를 사칭한 피싱 메일을 통해 원격제어 악성코드를 유포하는 사례가 지속적으로 탐지됨 ([이스트시큐리티 알약](https://blog.alyac.co.kr/5771)).

### 4. 주요 CVE / 취약점
- **CVE-2026-48449**: Adobe Campaign Classic, CVSS 10.0, 원격 코드 실행 가능 ([데일리시큐](https://www.dailysecu.com/news/articleView.html?idxno=207877))
- **Active Storage Flaw (Rails)**: Ruby on Rails, Critical, 임의 파일 읽기 및 RCE 가능 ([BleepingComputer](https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/rails-patches-critical-active-storage-flaw-with-rce-potential/))

### 5. IOC 요약
- **CVE**: CVE-2026-48449 ([데일리시큐](https://www.dailysecu.com/news/articleView.html?idxno=207877)), CVE-2026-67599 ([Twitter/LazyTitan33](https://twitter.com/LazyTitan33/status/2083325372838347257)), CVE-2026-15241 ([CVEnew](https://twitter.com/CVEnew/status/2083848557841551494))
- **해시**: 이번 수집 데이터 내 직접적인 파일 해시값은 제공되지 않음.

### 6. 즉각 대응 권고
- **패치 적용**: Adobe Campaign Classic 및 Ruby on Rails 환경의 최신 보안 업데이트를 즉시 적용하여 RCE 취약점 제거.
- **클라우드 보안 강화**: 제3자 클라우드 서비스 제공업체에 저장된 데이터에 대한 접근 제어 및 IAM 키 관리 정책 재점검 (Amgen 사례 참조).
- **하드웨어 지갑 점검**: Coldcard 등 하드웨어 지갑 사용 시 최신 펌웨어 업데이트 여부를 확인하고, 난수 생성 관련 보안 권고 사항 준수.

### 7. 위협 수준 평가
- **점수**: 8/10
- **근거**: CVSS 10.0 수준의 취약점과 하드웨어 지갑을 통한 대규모 자산 탈취, 국가 배후 조직의 랜섬웨어 공격이 동시에 보고되어 기업 및 개인의 보안 위협이 매우 높은 상태임.
